input.question: why do some roller coasters exhaust their lifespan in 8-10 years while others made of the same materials last 40+ at the same parks?
input.ground_truth: Most short lived coasters tend to have significant g forces that put extra stress on the structure. This causes harder wear on the rails, substructure, and train components. If the coaster has a unique or complex mechanism (tilt coasters, original LIM, launchers, etc) it will most likely have life span issues due to those components failing more and more with age.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: why do some roller coasters exhaust their lifespan in 8-10 years while others made of the same materials last 40+ at the same parks?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, imagine you have two toy cars made from the same plastic. One you play with every single day, zooming it down ramps and crashing it into things. The other you only play with once in a while, and you keep it on a shelf when you’re not using it.

The toy car you play with a lot will get worn out faster, right? Its wheels might break, the paint might chip, and it might stop working after just a couple of years.

Roller coasters are a bit like that. Even if they’re made of the same stuff, some are used way more often. More people ride them every day, which makes the parts wear out faster. Also, some roller coasters might go faster, have more twists and turns, or be a little rougher, which makes them wear out quicker too.

Other roller coasters might not be as popular, or maybe they don’t go as fast or have as many loops. So, they don’t get used as much, and their parts don’t wear out as quickly. That’s why some roller coasters need to be replaced after just a few years, while others can keep running for a long, long time—even if they’re made of the same materials!
